newsitem.title: USA: New television season fails to excite viewers.
newsitem.headline: New television season fails to excite viewers.

text.p: If the hype that preceded the new fall television season were any indication of things to come, the networks would now be basking in glowing reviews.

Instead, they are retooling their new shows, reshuffling their schedules, and waiting, more than a month into the season, for something to emerge as a breakout hit like the "NYPD Blue" and "Friends" sensations of past years.

A handful of new shows, like ABC's "Spin City" have won critical praise and others, like NBC's "Suddenly Susan" are getting good ratings despite lukewarm reviews. But overall, the enthusiasm over this year's new programming pales against the popularity of a number of ageing hits like "Seinfeld".

Of three new comedies launched by the Fox network, "Lush Life" has already been cancelled in the wake of dismal reviews and a second, "Party Girl" has been put on hold. ABC announced Monday it was temporarily pulling three series -- "Coach", "Second Noah" and "Common Law" -- from its Saturday night lineup and running movies in their place.
Other networks have had better luck keeping shows on the air so far, but are getting more credit for the gimmicks used to reel in viewers than for the basic strength of their new offerings.

If past launches like "ER" or "Chicago Hope" won large audiences on the merit of the writing and performances, this year's formula for success appears to be based on resurrecting stars from popular shows of the past, and imitating tried and true formats.

The popular Fox science fiction drama, "The X-Files", for example, has spawned a group of copycat shows this year such as "Profiler" and "Dark Skies" on NBC and "Millenium" on Fox. Films from last year, including "Clueless" and "Dangerous Minds" have also been recycled into television series.
"There are a lot of derivative shows," said one Los Angeles television critic. "There is a general sense it is a fairly mediocre year in terms of development."
"I think of 42 or 43 new shows this year, most are disappointing," added Chuck Bachrach, executive vice president of media resources for Rubin Postaer and Associates in Santa Monica, Calif.

Chicago advertising agency Leo Burnett surveys viewers to get a sense of where to place commercials, and recently issued a report card on the new season. It graded six of the most talked-about new shows, but gave only one A, to "Spin City", in which Michael J. Fox plays deputy mayor of New York.

The agency gave a D to "Townies," the series starring former teen film star Molly Ringwald, and an F to "Clueless." The Brooke Shields sitcom "Suddenly Susan" squeaked by with a C plus, but the agency also noted that Shields' performance in early episodes "fell flat."

"This year probably doesn't have as many breakout kinds of programmes," said Jayne Spittler, director of media research at Burnett. "It's hard to look at the schedule and say, 'Wow, there are four or five new programmes that everyone wants to watch.'"
The mediocrity might be less striking were it not for the relentless promotion and discussion of the new season over the summer, which convinced many viewers they were in for something special.

That period included constant advertising by NBC during its telecast of the Olympics; hype at CBS over the stable of former television stars including Bill Cosby, Ted Danson and Rhea Perlman it had signed; and at ABC the arrival of Jamie Tarses, the former NBC executive known as the brain behind that network's "must see" lineup.
"The promos were better than the shows at NBC," said Bachrach. Other critics have asked, not entirely in jest, if the networks drained their best creative talent on promotion.

They say the combination of promoting to the hilt and then following through with safe, unoriginal programming, reflected the increasingly competitive nature of the business. With an explosion of cable stations offering viewers more options, networks have to work harder to get their shows noticed but are all the more wary of gambling on something unusual.

"Last year was weak," said Bachrach, recalling the trend of that season to launch "Friends" lookalikes. "This year is weaker and next year may be the weakest. I don't know where the networks are going."
